segments.t: Outside in the courtyard the next morning, Viktor Barinov approaches Dmitry Nagiyev's car to ask permission for the TV shoot, but quickly realizes Nagiyev will be away on set all day. Let's listen to their Russian exchange first.
Меня не будет, я весь день на съёмках.
Now let's go back through their exchange line by line and unpack the Russian phrasing.
'What are you doing out here?' Spoken Russian keeps this brief and expressive, built right around 'are doing' without extra helper words.
'Dima, hi. What are you doing?' Chef Viktor addresses the listener with the informal singular pronoun, showing a close or familiar relationship.
'Oh, nothing much.' In spoken Russian, a compact phrase like this carries the full meaning through tone and context.
'What do you mean, nothing?' Chef Viktor raises the pitch on the key word to turn this short Russian clause into a direct question.
'I have that important guest today, remember?' Dmitry uses the first-person pronoun in the case required by the Russian verb or preposition.
'Of course I remember.' Here Chef Barinov anchors the thought on 'of course, certainly' and finishes on 'remember', keeping the spoken rhythm brisk and natural.
Меня не будет, я весь день на съёмках.

'I won't be here, I'm at a shoot all day.' Putting the short word for 'not' right in front of the action word is all Russian needs to make a sentence negative, with no extra helper words like 'do' or 'did'.
'Everything is counting on you.' Dmitry addresses the listener with the informal singular pronoun, showing a close or familiar relationship.
'Mind you don't mess up.' Notice how Russian puts 'don't' and 'watch' together in a short, direct phrase where word endings show how the ideas connect.
'Come on over.' Chef Barinov centers this short reply on 'to come, to arrive', letting a few direct words carry the whole meaning.
'I reached an agreement with Nagiyev.' In everyday Russian, 'agreement' flows straight into 'made a deal, agreed' without extra linking words.

'I am waiting for you in the kitchen.' Chef Viktor uses the polite plural form of address to maintain a respectful or ironic distance. Now let's hear the entire conversation once more from start to finish.
Меня не будет, я весь день на съёмках.
That finishes the parking-lot exchange between Viktor and Dmitry Nagiyev before the television crew returns. Listen for how everyday Russian drops the present-tense verb 'to be'. Until next time!
